headline: He stopped the Bend school shooter. He can't sleep.
summary: Kaylub Giamanco, a carpenter whose daughters attend Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, shot and killed the 16-year-old who attacked the school on October 15. Three boys, aged 5, 8 and 11, and a teacher had already died. In his first interview, with Oregon Public Broadcasting, he said: "I want to apologise for not saving their babies."

cover_question.q: Why does the hero feel guilty?

cover_answer: He got there after four people had died. He counts them.
table_question: Can you be brave and still feel you failed?

5-7.script: A dad in Oregon stopped someone who was hurting people at a school, and the police say he saved many children. He is very sad, because he could not get there in time to save everyone. Brave and sad fit in the same person, like being tired after a long, hard run. Your school has grown-ups whose whole job is keeping you safe.
5-7.why: Brave and sad in one person. The runner makes it concrete.
5-7.why_long: A child this age reads your face before your words and takes one vivid detail for the whole event, so the script never gives them the shotgun or the classroom. It gives them a tired runner and the grown-ups at their own school. Shielded: raise it only if they heard it first. Expect "could that happen at my school?" Say the grown-ups train.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Kaylub Giamanco was passing his daughters' school when he saw a teenager with a shotgun. He called 911, then went in, because waiting meant more people would die. A teacher had tackled the gunman, which gave him a clear shot. Like a fire drill: the plan exists because there's no time.
8-12.why: The school, a shotgun, a call, a tackle, a shot. One chain.
8-12.why_long: At this age a child builds chains of cause and effect and checks them for fairness, so the script gives the chain in order: the school, the shotgun, the 911 call, the teacher's tackle, the shot. The fire drill is a mechanism they already run. Expect "why does he feel bad if he won?" Because he counts the four he was too late for.

13-17.script: Does being a hero mean you feel like one? Kaylub Giamanco killed the 16-year-old who had shot three boys and a teacher at his daughters' school, and says the ones he didn't save are what he thinks about. Second: he had a handgun in his truck, legally. Does this change your view, or confirm it?
13-17.why: He saved children and lies awake. The gun question is theirs.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: this man saved children, and he lies awake seeing faces. The script asks them to hold both, then puts the gun question to them straight, because they will meet it online whichever way they lean. Kuhn's point: arguing is a skill, and it improves against someone honest. Expect "so, for or against?"

5-7.a: Yes. He said his chest hurt the whole time. Brave people get scared too. They keep going anyway.

8-12.q: Why does the hero feel guilty?
8-12.a: He got there after three boys and a teacher had died. He counts them.

8-12.q: Should he have waited for the police?
8-12.a: He told 911 people would die, and went in. Police say he saved lives.

13-17.q: Was it right to shoot a 16-year-old?
13-17.a: He had killed four and was reaching for his gun. Giamanco calls it a weight.

13-17.q: Does this prove more guns would help?
13-17.a: It is one case. The unarmed teacher who tackled him is in the same story.
